screens.title: What is a cryptographic hash function?
screens.narratorSegment: A cryptographic hash function is a deterministic mathematical procedure that maps data of arbitrary size to a fixed-size output called a hash or digest. In Bitcoin the canonical example is SHA-256, which always produces a 256-bit result represented as a 64-character hexadecimal string. The function is deterministic: the same input produces the same hash every time. It is one-way or preimage resistant, meaning you cannot feasibly recover the original input from the hash alone. Collision resistance means it is computationally impractical to find two distinct inputs that yield the same hash. Finally, the avalanche effect ensures a tiny change to input leads to a dramatically different hash. Together these properties make hashes ideal for integrity checks, unique identifiers for transactions, and linking blocks: each block stores the hash of the previous block header, forming an immutable chain. A common misconception is to treat a hash like encrypted data; unlike encryption, a hash does not permit recovery of the original content. To make this concrete, practice with short strings and observe identical inputs producing identical hashes and small edits producing completely different outputs. How does this immutability help you reason about tamper-evidence on the blockchain?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A hash function produces a fixed-size, one-way digest used for integrity, identification, and chaining in Bitcoin.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › What is a cryptographic hash function?
Definition

Cryptographic hash function

Maps data of any size to a fixed-size digest. Key properties ensure integrity and tamper evidence on the blockchain.

Deterministic: same input, same output every time.
One-way: infeasible to reverse a hash to find the input.
Collision resistance: hard to find two inputs with the same output.
Avalanche effect: tiny input change yields an unpredictable different hash.
Key Takeaway

Hashes are integrity tools: they prove data has not been altered and provide compact identifiers in Bitcoin.

Analogy & example
Think of a hash as a tamper-evident fingerprint for data. If the fingerprint changes, the data changed. This is why blocks link together: the previous block's fingerprint is embedded in the next block header, creating an unalterable history.
Common misconception
Hashes are not encryption. Encryption is reversible with a key; hashing intentionally discards recoverable structure to provide one-way integrity.
Try this mentally
  • Pick a sentence and imagine a unique 256-bit fingerprint: change one word and the fingerprint becomes unrelated.
  • Consider how storing the previous fingerprint in the next block prevents undetected edits.

screens.title: SHA-256 in action — concrete hashes
screens.narratorSegment: Seeing concrete hash outputs makes abstract properties real. When we hash the exact string "Hello Cohortia!" using SHA-256 we get a consistent 256-bit digest represented as 64 hexadecimal characters. If we change just one character — for example lowercasing the initial letter — the resulting hash is completely different. This demonstrates both determinism and the avalanche effect. Determinism means repeating the exact input yields the same digest each time; the avalanche effect shows that tiny input edits produce unpredictable outputs. In practice, Bitcoin uses these behaviors when producing transaction IDs and linking blocks. A common error is to assume similar inputs lead to similar hashes; the opposite is true. Practice by hashing short and long inputs and confirm the fixed output length. When teaching or auditing, record both the input and its digest so you can reproduce checks exactly. Why does this matter? Because reproducible, one-way fingerprints let every node independently verify data integrity without trusting an authority. SHA-256 in action — concrete hashes means small input changes create totally different sha-256 outputs; identical inputs always produce the same digest.. In practical terms, observe determinism and the avalanche effect with real sha-256 outputs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Small input changes create totally different SHA-256 outputs; identical inputs always produce the same digest.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › SHA-256 in action
Code example
Input: Hello Cohortia!
SHA-256: 22649622d100c50495f87b212f4553d100808a1599557404494a37f2619c922a

Input: hello Cohortia!
SHA-256: 312c019a164e62551525a74a12398d89e02c6110f0119e70195a6f2b45053075
What to notice
  • Both outputs are 64 hex characters representing 256 bits; size is fixed regardless of input length.
  • The two hashes are completely different despite a single-character case change in the input.
  • Re-entering the exact original input reproduces the same hash every time due to determinism.
Misconception check
Do not assume hashes are compressions you can reverse; they are one-way fingerprints.
Practical notes
Use hash outputs as compact, reproducible identifiers. When auditing transactions or blocks, keep the exact input string and hashing algorithm to reproduce results reliably. Small changes in whitespace or case will alter the digest completely, so exactness matters.
Example use in Bitcoin
SHA-256 appears in transaction IDs, block header hashing, and as a step in address derivation alongside RIPEMD-160.
Key Takeaway

Determinism and the avalanche effect together make SHA-256 a reliable fingerprint for verifying unchanged data across nodes.

screens.title: Hashing versus encryption
screens.narratorSegment: Hashing and encryption are both cryptographic tools but they serve different purposes and behave differently. Hashing, as used with SHA-256 in Bitcoin, is one-way: it converts data into a fixed digest intended for integrity checks and identification, not for concealment. Encryption is reversible: data is transformed so that only someone with the correct decryption key can recover the original content. A common mistake is to think that hashing protects confidentiality; it does not. Hashes do not hide data, they only provide a compact verification that data has not been changed. For example, you might hash a block header to produce a fingerprint; this does not obscure the block’s content. By contrast, encryption would be used when you need to keep data secret and recover it later. For Bitcoin, hashing enforces tamper evidence and linking, while signatures and public-key schemes provide authentication without revealing secrets. Understanding this contrast prevents incorrect security designs and misapplied tools. Hashing versus encryption means hashing is one-way integrity; encryption is reversible confidentiality — they are not interchangeable.. In practical terms, clarifying the common confusion: one-way integrity vs reversible confidentiality. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Hashing vs Encryption
Comparison
Hashing (one-way)
Fixed-size digest, not reversible, used for integrity, identification and linking.
Encryption (two-way)
Transforms data to hide content; requires a key to decrypt and recover the original data.
Concrete contrast
  • Hashing: verify that a downloaded file has not been changed by comparing digests.
  • Encryption: keep a message confidential so only the holder of the key can read it.
Misuse warning
Do not rely on hashing to protect private data — hashed values can be brute-forced if inputs are low entropy.
Why this matters for Bitcoin
Bitcoin uses hashing to make data tamper-evident and compact identifiers. It does not encrypt transaction data. Privacy requires different techniques; the blockchain remains a public ledger of hashed and signed transactions.
Key Takeaway

Use hashing for integrity and linking; use encryption when you must keep content recoverable only by authorized parties.

screens.title: How Bitcoin uses SHA-256
screens.narratorSegment: SHA-256 appears in multiple places inside Bitcoin. The process can be viewed in three common roles. First, transaction IDs are produced by hashing transaction data; this yields a compact identifier that nodes use to reference transactions. Second, blocks are linked through hashes: a block header contains the hash of the previous block header, so any change in history alters subsequent hashes and breaks the chain. Third, hashing is part of address derivation — public keys are hashed (together with additional steps) to produce addresses you share to receive bitcoin. The practical effect is that hashes make data compact and tamper-evident, enabling independent verification by all nodes. A typical misunderstanding is to think hashing conceals transaction content — it does not; transactions remain publicly visible, but hashes provide a verifiable fingerprint. These uses collectively support immutability, indexing, and address generation in Bitcoin's protocol. How Bitcoin uses SHA-256 means used for transaction ids, block linking, and as a step in deriving bitcoin addresses from public keys.. In practical terms, from transaction ids to block linking and address derivation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: SHA-256 roles
keyIdea.text: Used for transaction IDs, block linking, and as a step in deriving Bitcoin addresses from public keys.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › How Bitcoin uses SHA-256
Process
  1. Transaction ID: transaction data hashed to produce an identifier nodes reference when checking UTXOs.
  2. Block linking: each block header includes the previous header's hash, forming an immutable chain if headers are untampered.
  3. Address derivation: public keys are hashed (SHA-256 and then RIPEMD-160 in typical flows) and encoded to create a shareable address.
Key Takeaway
These roles make SHA-256 central to indexing, tamper evidence, and compact address construction.
Annotated examples
Transaction ID
Nodes use the transaction hash to find referenced unspent outputs and verify funds when processing new transactions.
Block header
Including the previous header's hash means any change to an earlier block changes all following headers' hashes.
Address derivation note
Address creation uses hashing as a step. The address is a derived, shareable identifier produced by hashing and encoding a public key.

screens.title: Private key → Public key → Bitcoin address
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the relationship between private keys, public keys, and addresses is central to Bitcoin ownership. A private key is a very large random number kept secret. From this private key a public key is derived mathematically; the public key can be shared freely because it does not allow reconstruction of the private key. The Bitcoin address you give someone to receive funds comes from hashing and encoding that public key. The key hierarchy is therefore private key controls funds, public key verifies signatures and allows address derivation, and the address acts as the visible identifier to receive bitcoin. A common misconception is to treat addresses as secrets — addresses are intended to be shared. However, the link back to a public key may reveal information on chain when you spend; understanding derivation helps reason about privacy. Practice tracing this chain conceptually for a single keypair to see which artifacts are secret, which are shareable, and which are public on the ledger. Private key → Public key → Bitcoin address means private key is secret; public key is derived and safe to share; addresses are derived and used to receive funds.. In practical terms, trace how ownership flows from a secret number to a shareable address. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Private key is secret; public key is derived and safe to share; addresses are derived and used to receive funds.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Private → Public → Address
Hierarchy
Private key: a secret large random number. Control equals access to funds.
Public key: derived from the private key mathematically; used for verification and address derivation.
Bitcoin address: derived by hashing and encoding the public key; shared to receive bitcoin.
Privacy note
An address is shareable, but once you spend from it the public key may become visible and reduce privacy. Understand derivation to manage exposure.
Annotated chain
Secret
Private key — never reveal.
Derived
Public key — used to verify signatures and derive addresses.
Shareable
Bitcoin address — give to others to receive funds.
Practice tracing: for one private key, identify which artifacts you would store offline, which you might publish in a transaction, and which you can safely give to someone to receive bitcoin.

screens.title: Public-key cryptography and ownership
screens.narratorSegment: Public-key cryptography uses a pair of mathematically linked keys: a private key kept secret and a public key that can be shared. The private key allows you to create a digital signature on data; the public key allows anyone to verify that signature. This asymmetric relationship is what makes ownership verifiable without revealing the secret that grants control. In Bitcoin, the private key authorizes spending. When a transaction is signed with the private key, nodes use the included public key and the signature to confirm the authorization. This process does not reveal the private key itself. The architecture centers on trustless verification: any node can check that the signature corresponds to the public key and that the public key derives from a known address if needed. The practical implication is that keys are both cryptographic tools and threat-model decisions: the security of your funds depends entirely on keeping the private key secret and using secure signing methods. What would happen if the private key is exposed? The attacker gains control of the funds — this is why key management is paramount.

keyIdea.title: Asymmetric trust
keyIdea.text: Private keys sign; public keys verify. This enables anyone to confirm ownership claims without access to secrets.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Public-key cryptography
Architecture
A private key signs, a public key verifies. This asymmetric design lets any node validate a signature without gaining control.
Signature generation
Create a signature using the private key over the specific transaction data to be authorized.
Signature verification
Use the public key and the signature to mathematically check authenticity and that the signer controlled the private key.
Threat model
If the private key is exposed, the attacker can sign transactions and spend the funds. Keep the private key secret and prefer hardware signing where possible.
Concrete analogy
Think of the private key as a sealed stamp only you possess. The public key is the imprint anyone can check. The stamp itself never has to be shown to prove the imprint is authentic.
Key Takeaway
Asymmetric cryptography lets a decentralized network validate ownership claims without central trust, provided private keys remain secret.

screens.title: Creating and verifying a digital signature
screens.narratorSegment: Digital signatures are the mechanism that proves you authorized a Bitcoin spend. The signing process starts when you build a transaction: you select unspent outputs, set outputs and amounts, and create the transaction data to be authorized. Your wallet uses your private key to create a signature specific to that transaction. The transaction is then broadcast along with your public key and the signature. Nodes receive the broadcast and take two main actions: they verify the signature using the provided public key to ensure the signature matches the transaction data and the public key, and they check your referenced unspent outputs to confirm you have sufficient funds. If both checks pass, the transaction is accepted into the mempool. A key misconception is that the public key alone proves ownership; it only verifies a signature created with the private key. keyIdea.text: Sign transaction data with a private key; nodes verify the signature with the public key and check UTXOs before accepting the transaction.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Signing and verification
Steps to sign
  1. Select UTXOs you control and create transaction outputs.
  2. Create the transaction data to be authorized (inputs, outputs, amounts).
  3. Use your private key to produce a digital signature over that transaction data.
  4. Broadcast the transaction with your public key and signature to the network.
Verification
Nodes verify the signature with the public key and confirm the UTXOs are unspent and sufficient.
Concrete scenario
Imagine you sign a 0.5 BTC payment. Your wallet uses your private key to sign that exact payment. When broadcast, every node can confirm you authorized that specific transfer without ever seeing your private key. If verification passes and the UTXOs exist, the network accepts the transaction.
Misconception check
A signature proves authorization for that transaction only; it does not reveal the private key or allow new signatures to be forged without the private key.

screens.title: Alice sends 0.5 BTC — transaction walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the exact scenario from the chapter: Alice wants to send 0.5 BTC to Bob. First, her wallet constructs a transaction that references specific unspent transaction outputs she controls. The transaction lists Bob's receiving address and the amount, and includes references to Alice's UTXOs. Next, Alice's wallet signs that transaction data with her private key, producing a digital signature tied to that transaction. The wallet then broadcasts the signed transaction together with Alice's public key and the signature. Nodes on the network receive the broadcast and run two checks: they verify the signature with Alice's public key to ensure the signature is valid for that transaction and they confirm that the referenced UTXOs are unspent and sufficient to cover 0.5 BTC. If both checks pass, the transaction is relayed and eventually included in a block. A misconception sometimes seen is thinking public keys alone transfer funds — the public key only verifies a signature; the private key is required to create that signature. Consider what step would fail if Alice used the wrong private key or referenced already spent UTXOs.

screens.title: ECDSA — the signature algorithm Bitcoin uses
screens.narratorSegment: Bitcoin uses the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm to produce and verify signatures. Conceptually, ECDSA is a way to create a signature from a private key such that anyone with the corresponding public key can check the signature’s validity. Elliptic curve methods provide strong security with relatively small key sizes compared to older systems. In practice this means a private key on Bitcoin is a compact large number, and ECDSA produces signatures that bind that private key to a specific transaction. Importantly, ECDSA ensures signatures cannot be used to recover the private key. A common oversight is to conflate signature verification with spending: verification only proves that the signature corresponds to the public key; the actual control of funds still depends on whether the UTXOs are unspent. For learners, the critical point is functional: ECDSA lets the network validate that an authorized party signed a transaction without exposing the secret key that would allow others to sign. Reflect on how smaller key sizes yet strong security helps with storage and transmission efficiency on a global public ledger. content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › ECDSA overview
Definition
ECDSA is the elliptic-curve-based algorithm Bitcoin uses to create and verify digital signatures. It allows compact keys and signatures while delivering strong security guarantees against forgery and private key recovery when used correctly.
Purpose: authenticate a transaction without revealing the private key.
Property: signatures are bound to specific transaction data, preventing reuse for different transactions.
Benefit: efficient cryptography with small storage and bandwidth footprint.
Key Takeaway
ECDSA is the practical signature scheme enabling secure, verifiable authorization in Bitcoin using elliptic-curve math.
Practical note
You do not need to implement ECDSA to use Bitcoin; wallet software handles keys and signing. Your role is to protect the private key and understand that signatures prove authorization without exposing secrets.
Misconception
Verifying a signature does not mean the verifier can create signatures; it only confirms the signer had the private key at signing time.

screens.title: Private key management — safety practices
screens.narratorSegment: Private key management is the most practical security issue for anyone using Bitcoin. The rule is simple and uncompromising: your private key controls access to funds. If you lose the private key, you lose access; if you share it, you share control. Best practices include storing private keys on secure, offline devices or hardware wallets designed to sign transactions without exposing the secret. Avoid storing private keys on internet-connected devices, do not photograph or email them, and prefer deterministic wallet backups that you can restore from secure seed phrases. Hardware wallets help by keeping signing within the device so the private key never leaves secure storage. A common human error is treating backups casually; record recovery seeds securely and test your recovery process with small funds before moving large amounts. Understand that no cryptographic trick will recover funds if a private key is permanently lost — custody discipline is the final line of defense. keyIdea.title: Safety first
keyIdea.text: Private keys must be kept secret and backed up securely; hardware wallets and offline storage reduce the risk of theft or loss.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Private key management
Best practices
  • Use hardware wallets for significant balances so signing happens on-device.
  • Keep backups of recovery seeds in secure, geographically separated locations.
  • Avoid digital copies of private keys on cloud storage or email.
  • Test your recovery procedure with small amounts before transferring large funds.
Consequence
Losing your private key is irreversible: there is no central authority to restore access to funds.
Practical checklist
Prefer hardware wallets for signing and keep the seed phrase offline.
Don’t reuse single backups in multiple insecure places; spread risk across safe locations.
Never share private keys; treat them like the single secret to your holdings.
Key Takeaway
Good key custody practices are as important as cryptographic strength — human choices determine whether cryptography protects your funds.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will build an intuitive and practical understanding of the cryptographic building blocks that make Bitcoin secure. You will learn what cryptographic hash functions do, why SHA-256 is essential for transaction integrity and block linking, and how public-key cryptography enables ownership and the digital signatures that authorize spends. Along the way we’ll see concrete examples, including two different SHA-256 outputs that illustrate the avalanche effect, and a walkthrough of how a transaction gets signed and verified. We will also highlight a common mistake — confusing hashing with encryption — and conclude with clear private key safety practices. These ideas are not abstract rules; they are the mechanisms that let a decentralized network verify transactions without trusting any central party. By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain how hashes provide integrity, how key pairs prove ownership, and why the single secret — the private key — must be protected. Think of this as the cryptographic toolkit for owning and moving bitcoin safely.

These objectives map directly to the cryptographic principles that secure Bitcoin. First, you will explain the core properties of cryptographic hash functions, focusing on SHA-256: determinism, one-way behavior, collision resistance, and the avalanche effect. Understanding these properties helps you see why hashes can identify transactions and tie blocks together reliably. Second, you'll describe public-key cryptography: how a private key and a derived public key work together to prove ownership without exposing the secret. Third, you will illustrate digital signatures: how a private key signs a transaction and how the network uses the public key to verify that signature. Fourth, you'll understand the relationship between keys and addresses — how an address is derived from a public key and serves as the shareable identifier for receiving bitcoin. Each objective includes a short competency milestone so you can self-verify your understanding. Together these skills allow you to reason about transaction integrity, ownership claims, and practical safety measures for private key custody.

This second objectives slide turns toward applied skills and safety. First, you will identify critical security practices for private key management: never disclose your private key, avoid insecure storage, and prefer hardware wallets for long-term custody. Second, you will practice describing how a Bitcoin address is derived from a public key using hashing steps — this helps you reason about what an address reveals and what it conceals. Third, you will gain the ability to walk through a signing workflow: creating a transaction, signing it with a private key, broadcasting it, and watching nodes verify the signature against the public key. Fourth, you will be able to contrast hashing and encryption clearly, avoiding a common misconception that hashes are reversible. Each card here represents a measurable competency you can speak about and check during hands-on exercises. These practice goals ensure you can not only explain theory but also apply secure habits and verify transaction authenticity in practical scenarios.

A cryptographic hash function is a deterministic mathematical procedure that maps data of arbitrary size to a fixed-size output called a hash or digest. In Bitcoin the canonical example is SHA-256, which always produces a 256-bit result represented as a 64-character hexadecimal string. The function is deterministic: the same input produces the same hash every time. It is one-way or preimage resistant, meaning you cannot feasibly recover the original input from the hash alone. Collision resistance means it is computationally impractical to find two distinct inputs that yield the same hash. Finally, the avalanche effect ensures a tiny change to input leads to a dramatically different hash. Together these properties make hashes ideal for integrity checks, unique identifiers for transactions, and linking blocks: each block stores the hash of the previous block header, forming an immutable chain. A common misconception is to treat a hash like encrypted data; unlike encryption, a hash does not permit recovery of the original content. To make this concrete, practice with short strings and observe identical inputs producing identical hashes and small edits producing completely different outputs. How does this immutability help you reason about tamper-evidence on the blockchain?

Seeing concrete hash outputs makes abstract properties real. When we hash the exact string "Hello Cohortia!" using SHA-256 we get a consistent 256-bit digest represented as 64 hexadecimal characters. If we change just one character — for example lowercasing the initial letter — the resulting hash is completely different. This demonstrates both determinism and the avalanche effect. Determinism means repeating the exact input yields the same digest each time; the avalanche effect shows that tiny input edits produce unpredictable outputs. In practice, Bitcoin uses these behaviors when producing transaction IDs and linking blocks. A common error is to assume similar inputs lead to similar hashes; the opposite is true. Practice by hashing short and long inputs and confirm the fixed output length. When teaching or auditing, record both the input and its digest so you can reproduce checks exactly. Why does this matter? Because reproducible, one-way fingerprints let every node independently verify data integrity without trusting an authority. SHA-256 in action — concrete hashes means small input changes create totally different sha-256 outputs; identical inputs always produce the same digest.. In practical terms, observe determinism and the avalanche effect with real sha-256 outputs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Hashing and encryption are both cryptographic tools but they serve different purposes and behave differently. Hashing, as used with SHA-256 in Bitcoin, is one-way: it converts data into a fixed digest intended for integrity checks and identification, not for concealment. Encryption is reversible: data is transformed so that only someone with the correct decryption key can recover the original content. A common mistake is to think that hashing protects confidentiality; it does not. Hashes do not hide data, they only provide a compact verification that data has not been changed. For example, you might hash a block header to produce a fingerprint; this does not obscure the block’s content. By contrast, encryption would be used when you need to keep data secret and recover it later. For Bitcoin, hashing enforces tamper evidence and linking, while signatures and public-key schemes provide authentication without revealing secrets. Understanding this contrast prevents incorrect security designs and misapplied tools. Hashing versus encryption means hashing is one-way integrity; encryption is reversible confidentiality — they are not interchangeable.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. SHA-256 appears in multiple places inside Bitcoin. The process can be viewed in three common roles. Private key management is the most practical security issue for anyone using Bitcoin. The rule is simple and uncompromising: your private key controls access to funds. If you lose the private key, you lose access; if you share it, you share control. Best practices include storing private keys on secure, offline devices or hardware wallets designed to sign transactions without exposing the secret. Avoid storing private keys on internet-connected devices, do not photograph or email them, and prefer deterministic wallet backups that you can restore from secure seed phrases. Hardware wallets help by keeping signing within the device so the private key never leaves secure storage. A common human error is treating backups casually; record recovery seeds securely and test your recovery process with small funds before moving large amounts. Understand that no cryptographic trick will recover funds if a private key is permanently lost — custody discipline is the final line of defense.
